## 5. Interpretation (hand-written from the numbers above; not regenerated by the script)

**The runs agree; the references do not.** Every overlapping case reproduces eval_v2 (352/352) and the evolve track (40/40) exactly. On the same 25 bodies the wedge passes 5/25 against each body's own twin floor and 16/25 against the seed-0 body. All 11 disagreements go one way (fail against own, pass against seed 0); none goes the other way. Core excision does not depend on the reference (5/25 under both, the same 5 bodies). The evolve track's 1/10 core and 7/10 wedge and eval_v2's 4/21 and 4/21 are both reproduced. The differences come from the seed subsets and the reference, not from the simulator.

**Why the wedge flips.** The wedge removes the posterior third of the body, including P, and the regrown posterior is less seed-specific than the one it replaced. Before the cut, the P organizer row spans 26–32 across bodies (SD 2.32). After regrowth it spans the same range but with less spread (SD 1.42). Against its own pre-cut body every wedge case loses about the same amount (mean gap +0.0433 ± 0.0178). That gap does not depend on how close the body was to seed 0 (r = −0.214). Against seed 0, the floor itself is the body's cross-seed similarity to seed 0, which ranges from 0.8984 to 0.9757. The regrown bodies land between 0.9040 and 0.9589 against seed 0 whatever floor they started from (r = +0.263 with the floor). So:
- Bodies that started far from seed 0 (the 11 fail/pass cases, mean growth similarity to seed 0 of 0.9185) regrow a posterior that is more like seed 0's than their own was. Of the cells the wedge changed, 56.8% now agree with seed 0, so the ref0 gap is negative (mean −0.0090) and they "pass".
- Bodies that started close to seed 0 (the 9 fail/fail cases, mean 0.9627) have nothing to gain. Only 23.1% of their changed cells agree with seed 0, and they fail under both references.

The ref0 gap tracks the body's similarity to seed 0 (r = +0.821). So the seed-0 criterion mostly measures how far each body was from seed 0 to begin with. It does not measure whether the body restored its own form. A body that loses its individual posterior and regrows a generic one is penalised against its own twin and rewarded against a foreign reference whose floor is already low.

**Mechanism of the own-reference failure.** Before the cut, P sits in column 18 in 23 of 25 bodies. After regrowth only 7 of 25 are back in column 18; 18 of 25 re-form 1–2 blocks further from the core along the axis (columns 16–17; the core is at column 29). This is consistent with the radial degeneracy of P's score: if both signals decay as exp(−d/λ) along relay paths, ln C − ln A = (d_A − d_C)/λ, which is constant (= D/λ, D the A–core distance) at every point on the far side of the A–core axis, so the score fixes P's direction but not its distance from the core. (Derivation under idealised straight relay paths; readings are noisy and smoothed in the simulation.)

**Which verdict answers the paper's question.** Regeneration means restoring the body that was cut, so the own-twin reference is the right primary measure. The seed-0 reference is a useful second measure of plan fidelity, but it is not a repair test on its own. The wedge is a real defect: 5/25 (20%, Wilson 95% 9–39%) pass. The 7/10 figure comes from a reference whose floor varies by ±0.0287 across bodies, which is larger than the wedge defect itself.

**Growth similarity.** 0.946 (paper), 0.938 (eval_v2) and 0.928 (evolve track) are the same metric at the same step (t = 200) against the same seed-0 body. They come from three different seed sets: 1–10, 1–19 + 42 + 10000, and the evolve set, which includes four bodies (21, 42, 77, 10000) at 0.8952–0.9003. On the 25-body union the figure is 0.9376 ± 0.0290. The reference-free pairwise figure, each body against every other body, is 0.9343 ± 0.0082 (26 bodies), which matches eval_v2's 0.9340.
